full_title: HEIRS OF BENITA YANZON CIPRIANO, REPRESENTED BY MA. DOROTHY ARLENE CIPRIANO, PETITIONERS, VS. NATIONAL TRANSMISSION CORPORATION (TRANSCO), RESPONDENT.

doctrine:
**Just compensation is determined as of the date of the taking of the property or the filing of the complaint, whichever came first (Rule 67, Section 4).** This general rule applies even in inverse condemnation, where the government entered without filing expropriation proceedings. *NPC v. Heirs of Macabangkit Sangkay* and *NPC v. Saludares* reckoned value from the owner's filing of the inverse condemnation suit. Those rulings are exceptions justified only by special circumstances: stealth (underground tunnels the owners did not know of), or the expropriator's refusal to acknowledge the claim because it insisted it had already paid. They do not apply to **visible high-tension transmission lines**, whose existence the owners cannot claim to be unaware of. This is especially so where the expropriator invokes a right of way granted by the owner's predecessor. Reiterated (*NTC v. Oroville*; *NTC v. Religious of the Virgin Mary*).

The value at the time of taking must be computed with the **present value formula** of *Republic v. Spouses Nocom* and *Heirs of Jose Mariano v. City of Naga* (En Banc), which accounts for the owner's opportunity loss from non-payment. The total just compensation then earns 6% legal interest from the finality of the decision fixing it until full payment. **Consequential damages to the remaining portions are a component of just compensation.** They are likewise reckoned from the taking under the same formula.

The government's failure to file expropriation proceedings before taking the property ("construct first, expropriate later") warrants **exemplary damages and attorney's fees** (Civil Code, Arts. 2229 and 2208). The Court fixed them at PHP 1,000,000 and PHP 200,000. Rule 67, Section 12, which charges costs to the plaintiff, presupposes that the expropriator is the plaintiff. In an inverse condemnation suit filed by the owner, **the expropriator pays the costs**.
facts:
On July 21, 2015, the heirs of Benita Yanzon Cipriano sued the National Transmission Corporation (TransCo) before the RTC of Legazpi City for inverse condemnation or just compensation, with damages. TransCo is the successor to the transmission functions of the National Power Corporation (NPC) under RA 9136. The heirs alleged that in 1977 NPC built high-tension transmission lines over their Lot Nos. 15870-B and 15939 in Villahermosa, Daraga, Albay, without their consent and without expropriation proceedings, and that their demands for payment went unheeded.

TransCo answered that NPC entered on the strength of a right of way granted by the heirs' predecessor, Trinidad P. Vda. De Yanzon, for PHP 1,074.71 (easement fee, pole and guy occupancy, and damaged improvements). It also argued that the claim was barred by prescription and laches, and that just compensation should be reckoned from the time of taking. The complaint was amended after TransCo admitted occupying a larger portion of Lot No. 15939.

The RTC found that the Daraga-Putiao 69kV lines, built in 1977, traversed 2,776 sq m of Lot No. 15870-B and 2,009 sq m of Lot No. 15939. The Daraga-Bacman 230kV lines, built in 1994, traversed another 1,709 sq m of Lot No. 15939, for a total of 6,494 sq m. Applying the *Macabangkit Sangkay* and *Saludares* exception, the RTC reckoned just compensation from the 2015 filing of the complaint. It adopted one commissioner's valuation with modification, pegging the fair market value at PHP 600 per sq m, and awarded PHP 100 per sq m as consequential damages for the remaining 39,688 sq m. Its September 6, 2019 decision fixed just compensation at PHP 700 per sq m (PHP 4,545,800) and awarded PHP 50,000 attorney's fees and PHP 200,000 exemplary damages. The interest was modified on reconsideration.

On November 16, 2020, the CA set aside the RTC ruling. Citing *Oroville*, it held that no special circumstance justified departing from the time-of-taking rule. It found that the appraisals, based on 2009 zonal values and 2012-2015 sales data, did not reflect values at the time of taking. It remanded the case for determination of just compensation, exemplary damages and attorney's fees, with 12% interest from taking until June 30, 2013 and 6% thereafter. The heirs filed a Rule 45 petition.
issues: Whether just compensation should be reckoned from the actual taking (1977 and 1994) rather than from the filing of the inverse condemnation complaint in 2015.
Whether consequential damages should be awarded.
Whether the heirs are entitled to increased exemplary damages and attorney's fees.
Whether TransCo should pay the costs of suit.
ruling:
The Court found it unnecessary to rule on the credibility of TransCo's evidence of the right-of-way grant, since it was established that no expropriation proceedings were filed when NPC entered.

**1. Yes. Just compensation is reckoned from the actual taking, but it is computed under the present value formula.** Rule 67, Section 4 fixes the value "as of the date of the taking of the property or the filing of the complaint, whichever came first." *Macabangkit Sangkay* and *Saludares* are exceptions grounded more on equity than on Rule 67. In *Macabangkit Sangkay*, NPC secretly built underground tunnels that the owners discovered only when a buyer backed out. In *Saludares*, NPC refused to acknowledge the claim, insisting it had already paid. As held in *Oroville* and *Religious of the Virgin Mary*, transmission lines are visible, and their very nature precludes "the expropriator's stealth and the owner's utter cluelessness." Here, TransCo also claimed entry under a right of way granted by Trinidad for PHP 1,074.71, which is analogous to the prescription claim in *Religious of the Virgin Mary*.

Applying the general rule does not condone taking without expropriation. Under *Heirs of Jose Mariano v. City of Naga*, applying *Spouses Nocom*, the value at taking is brought to its present value to compensate the owner's opportunity loss; this is distinct from legal interest for delay. **The remand was proper** because the RTC's valuation relied on 2009 zonal values and 2012-2015 sales data, not values at the time of taking. The total just compensation shall earn 6% legal interest from the finality of the decision fixing it until full payment.

**2. Yes. The RTC must determine them on remand.** Consequential damages are a component of just compensation (*NPC v. Marasigan*): the court ascertains the market value, adds the consequential damages, and deducts the consequential benefits. The RTC's earlier award was made in relation to a valuation the CA correctly set aside, so the RTC must redetermine it. It is reckoned from the taking, subject to the present value formula, and earns 6% interest from the finality of the decision fixing just compensation.

**3. Partly.** Exemplary damages (Art. 2229) and attorney's fees (Art. 2208) are awarded when a government agency illegally occupies private property for a long time without expropriation proceedings, causing the owner pecuniary loss (*Heirs of Mariano*, citing *Tecson* and *Manalastas*). Following *Heirs of Mariano*, *Tecson* and *Oroville*, the Court fixed **exemplary damages at PHP 1,000,000**. Following *Tecson*, *Oroville* and *Manalastas*, which all involved owners who sued after a taking without expropriation, it fixed **attorney's fees at PHP 200,000**. Both earn legal interest from the finality of the Decision. The heirs' prayer for PHP 3,000,000 exemplary damages and PHP 1,000,000 attorney's fees was not granted.

**4. Yes.** Rule 67, Section 12 charges costs to the plaintiff unless the owner appeals and the judgment is affirmed. That rule presupposes that the expropriator is the plaintiff. **Since NPC entered without filing expropriation proceedings, it would be unjust to make the owners pay the costs**; NPC or TransCo should have filed the case before taking the property. The Constitution forbids taking private property for public use without just compensation (Art. III, Sec. 9). The government's failure to expropriate may be corrected by exemplary damages, attorney's fees and costs of litigation.
disposition: The Petition was PARTIALLY GRANTED. The CA Decision of November 16, 2020 in CA-G.R. CV No. 114206 was AFFIRMED with MODIFICATION. Just compensation shall be reckoned from the actual taking: 1977 for the Daraga-Putiao 69kV lines (2,776 sq m of Lot No. 15870-B and 2,009 sq m of Lot No. 15939), and 1994 for the Daraga-Bacman 230kV lines (1,709 sq m of Lot No. 15939). Just compensation, including consequential damages for the remaining unoccupied portions, shall be determined under the formula in *Republic v. Spouses Nocom* and *Heirs of Jose Mariano v. City of Naga*, and shall earn 6% legal interest from the finality of the decision fixing it until full payment. TransCo was ordered to pay PHP 1,000,000 exemplary damages and PHP 200,000 attorney's fees, with 6% interest from the finality of the Decision. The case was remanded to RTC Branch 1, Legazpi City, for the determination of just compensation, consequential damages and costs of suit, with utmost dispatch. Costs against TransCo.

bar_questions.q: In 1985, the National Power Corporation built steel towers and high-tension transmission lines across a portion of Mario's ranch without filing an expropriation case. The towers are several stories high and visible from the highway. In 2024, Mario filed a complaint for just compensation (inverse condemnation) against the government corporation that succeeded NPC. He argues that because the government never expropriated, his land should be valued as of 2024, when he sued. The corporation claims that Mario's father granted NPC a right of way in 1985. As of what time should just compensation be reckoned?

alac.answer: Just compensation should be reckoned from the time of taking in 1985, but the 1985 value must be brought to present value using the present value formula.
alac.legal_basis: Under Rule 67, Section 4, just compensation is determined as of the date of the taking or the filing of the complaint, whichever came first. Reckoning from the filing of an inverse condemnation suit is an exception reserved for special circumstances, such as stealth or the expropriator's refusal to acknowledge the claim (Macabangkit Sangkay; Saludares). Visible transmission lines do not qualify. The value at taking is computed under the present value formula of Republic v. Spouses Nocom and Heirs of Jose Mariano v. City of Naga, and the total earns 6% legal interest from the finality of the decision fixing just compensation. (Heirs of Cipriano v. TransCo, G.R. No. 255113, August 6, 2025)
alac.application: The taking occurred in 1985, long before Mario sued in 2024. The towers are several stories high and visible, so there was no stealth, and Mario cannot claim he did not know of them. The corporation's claim of a right of way from Mario's father is a legal defense, not a refusal to acknowledge the facts of the taking. No special circumstance justifies the exception. Mario is still protected: the present value formula compensates for his lost opportunity to earn from the money since 1985, and he may also recover exemplary damages and attorney's fees for the failure to expropriate.
alac.conclusion: Just compensation is reckoned from the 1985 taking and computed under the present value formula.

bar_questions.q: In the 1970s, a government corporation secretly bored an underground water tunnel beneath Lorna's farm without informing her and without filing an expropriation case. Nothing on the surface showed the tunnel. Lorna discovered it only in 2023, when a buyer backed out of a sale after learning of it. She filed an inverse condemnation suit in 2024. May just compensation be based on the value of her land in 2024?

alac.answer: Yes. The case falls within the recognized exception, so just compensation may be reckoned from the filing of Lorna's complaint in 2024.
alac.legal_basis: The general rule under Rule 67, Section 4 reckons just compensation from the taking or the filing of the complaint, whichever came first. By way of exception, in NPC v. Heirs of Macabangkit Sangkay the Court reckoned it from the owners' filing of the inverse condemnation suit. There, NPC built underground tunnels without the owners' knowledge or consent, using stealth instead of expropriation, and the owners learned of them only when a buyer refused to proceed. Heirs of Cipriano v. TransCo (G.R. No. 255113, August 6, 2025) reaffirmed that this exception rests on such special circumstances, which are absent when the structures are visible.
alac.application: Unlike visible transmission lines, the tunnel was hidden underground, and Lorna was never informed of it. Like the owners in Macabangkit Sangkay, she learned of it only when a sale fell through. Valuing the land as of the 1970s would compound the unfairness caused by the corporation's stealth and let it profit from its denial of due process.
alac.conclusion: Lorna's just compensation may be based on the value of her land when she filed her inverse condemnation complaint in 2024.

bar_questions.q: On the facts of the first question, the trial court ruled for Mario. (a) Rule 67, Section 12 states that costs shall be paid by the plaintiff unless the owner appeals and the judgment is affirmed. Since Mario is the plaintiff, must he pay the costs? (b) May the court also award Mario exemplary damages and attorney's fees, even though his just compensation will already be adjusted to present value and earn interest?

alac.answer: (a) No. The government corporation, which should have filed the expropriation case, must pay the costs. (b) Yes. Exemplary damages and attorney's fees may be awarded for the government's failure to file expropriation proceedings before taking the land.
alac.legal_basis: Rule 67, Section 12 presupposes that the expropriator is the plaintiff. Where the owner had to sue because the government entered without expropriation, it would be unjust to charge the owner with the costs (see Const., Art. III, Sec. 9). Exemplary damages (Civil Code, Art. 2229) and attorney's fees (Art. 2208) may be awarded because of the government's long, illegal occupation of private property without expropriation proceedings, which causes the owner pecuniary loss. In Heirs of Cipriano v. TransCo (G.R. No. 255113, August 6, 2025), the Court ordered TransCo to pay the costs and awarded PHP 1,000,000 exemplary damages and PHP 200,000 attorney's fees.
alac.application: Mario is the plaintiff only because the government built its lines in 1985 without filing an expropriation case, so the costs fall on the government. The present value adjustment and legal interest compensate for the lost use of money and the delay in payment. Exemplary damages serve a different purpose: they correct the "construct first, expropriate later" practice for the public good. Attorney's fees are just and equitable because Mario was forced to litigate to be paid.
alac.conclusion: The government corporation must pay the costs, and Mario may recover exemplary damages and attorney's fees in addition to just compensation.

notes: First Division. Gesmundo, C.J. (Chairperson) and Hernando, J. concurred; Zalameda and Marquez, JJ. were on official business. In the part on consequential damages, the text says the RTC's "prior award of PHP 600.00 per square meter" was tied to the PHP 600 valuation. It apparently means the PHP 100 per sq m consequential damages, so the digest states the point generally.
